## Family Stories

Amy Ellen Provis married Francis Charles Telfer at Stokes in 1909 and together they raised ten children on a pioneering farm at Ungarra on the Eyre Peninsula. Life was brutally hard for her — no electricity, no running water, no refrigeration, no washing machine. She cooked on a wood stove, baked all the family's bread using homemade yeast made from hops, potatoes, flour and water, and made butter that she had to drive 18 miles into Tumby Bay in a sulky with one horse before the heat of the day. The money from the butter bought whatever groceries she could manage. She did the family laundry with a copper that had to be stoked with wood, two tubs, a scrubbing board and homemade soap, and ironed with a box iron full of hot coals. She carried water from the sheds in four-gallon kerosene tin buckets for all household needs. With a baby every couple of years, she somehow kept the household running through it all. Her daughters remembered that there was no entertainment as such in those days, "but plenty of hard work and just enough rest to keep us going." *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130–131)*

On **6 April 1909**, she married [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] at Stokes, South Australia. The wedding was reportedly covered by a local newspaper article — "Family Wedding at Jamestown" — which mentions the celebration.

Together they raised **ten children** on family farms, moving from the mid-north toward the Eyre Peninsula over the decades. Amy passed away in October 1951, predeceasing her husband Francis by about three years.

Her name appears in Murray John Telfer's profile as "Amy May" in some vault records, but her registered birth name is **Amy Ellen Provis**.

## Parents: The Provis & Thorpe Families

**George Provis** (Amy's father) — married **Emily Ellen Thorpe** on 15 June 1882. Emily's parents were **Charles Robert Thorpe** (1832–1893) and **Amelia White** (1833–1916).
